TargetRLF1: Here are some common misconceptions or myths about disability and adolescents:  1. Myth: Adolescents with disabilities are unable to lead independent lives. Reality: With appropriate support and accommodations, many adolescents with disabilities can live independently and make their own decisions.  2. Myth: Disability is a tragedy that needs to be cured. Reality: Disability is a natural part of human diversity, and adolescents with disabilities are not "broken" or in need of a "cure."  3. Myth: Adolescents with disabilities are not capable of sexual feelings or relationships. Reality: Adolescents with disabilities have the same sexual desires and needs as their peers and deserve access to comprehensive sex education and support.  4. Myth: Disability is only physical. Reality: Disability includes invisible disabilities like mental health conditions, chronic illnesses, and neurodiverse conditions.  5. Myth: Adolescents with disabilities are not capable of academic success. Reality: With appropriate support and accommodations, adolescents with disabilities can achieve academic success and pursue higher education.  6. Myth: Disability is a personal failing or result of poor parenting. Reality: Disability is a natural part of human diversity and not the result of personal or parental failures.  7. Myth: Adolescents with disabilities are not capable of making their own decisions. Reality: Adolescents with disabilities have the right to autonomy and self-determination, and should be supported in making their own decisions.  8. Myth: Disability is a limitation that needs to be overcome. Reality: Disability is a natural part of human diversity, and adolescents with disabilities should be valued and included for who they are.  9. Myth: Adolescents with disabilities are not capable of participating in sports or recreational activities. Reality: Adolescents with disabilities can participate in adaptive sports and recreational activities with appropriate support and accommodations.  10. Myth: Disability is a medical issue, not a social issue. Reality: Disability is both a medical and social issue, requiring a comprehensive approach to inclusion and accessibility.  It's essential to challenge these myths and misconceptions to create a more inclusive and supportive environment for adolescents with disabilities.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

The risk of HIV infection is related to behaviors and practices that expose individuals to the virus, rather than their blood type.

TargetRLF1: Chlamydia infections, also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary Infections, spread through sexual contact when vaginal fluid or semen containing the bacteria that cause chlamydia travels from one person to another. If you have had Chlamydia and you were treated in the past, you can get reinfected if you have unprotected sex with someone who has it.

TargetRLF1: The only way to completely avoid STIs is to not have vaginal, anal, or oral sex. If you are sexually active, you can do the following things to lower your chances of getting Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes:•        Being in a long-term mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who does not have herpes.•        Using condoms the right way every time you have sex.Be aware that not all herpes sores occur in areas that a condom can cover. Also, the skin can release the virus (shed) from areas that do not have a visible herpes sore. For these reasons, condoms may not fully protect you from getting herpes. If your sex partner(s) has/have genital herpes, you can lower your risk of getting it if:•        Your partner takes an anti-herpes medicine every day. This is something your partner should discuss with his or her healthcare provider.•        You avoid having vaginal, anal, or oral sex when your partner has herpes symptoms (i.e., during an "outbreak").If you are pregnant and have genital herpes, prenatal care visits are very important. Some research suggest that a genital herpes infection may lead to miscarriage or make it more likely to deliver your baby too early. You can pass herpes to your unborn child before birth, but it more commonly passes during delivery. This can lead to a deadly infection in your baby (called neonatal herpes). It is important that you avoid getting genital herpes during pregnancy. Tell your healthcare provider if you have ever had a genital herpes diagnosis or symptoms. Also tell them about any possible exposure to genital herpes. If you have genital herpes, you may need to take anti-herpes medicine towards the end of your pregnancy. This medicine may reduce your risk of having signs or symptoms of genital herpes when you deliver. At the time of delivery, your healthcare provider should carefully examine you for herpes sores. If you have signs or symptoms of genital herpes at delivery, a 'C-section' is likely to occur.

TargetRLF1: HSV-1 is mainly transmitted via contact with the virus in sores, saliva or surfaces in or around the mouth. Less commonly, HSV-1 can be transmitted to the genital area through oral-genital contact to cause Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes. It can be transmitted from oral or skin surfaces that appear normal; however, the greatest risk of transmission is when there are active sores. People who already have HSV-1 are not at risk of reinfection, but they are still at risk of acquiring HSV-2. HSV-2 is mainly transmitted during sex through contact with genital or anal surfaces, skin, sores or fluids of someone infected with the virus. HSV-2 can be transmitted even if the skin looks normal and is often transmitted in the absence of symptoms. In rare circumstances, herpes (HSV-1 and HSV-2) can be transmitted from mother to child during vaginal delivery, causing neonatal herpes.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis is treatable and it heals. People who suspect they may have syphilis should speak to their healthcare provider. The early stage of syphilis is treated with a benzathine penicillin (BPG) injection. As second line treatment, doctors may also use doxycycline, ceftriaxone or azithromycin, which are antibiotic medicines is also used to treat later stages of syphilis, but more doses are required. Doses are usually given once per week for three weeks, including when it is not possible to identify the stage of infection. Your partner should also get treatment. Do not have sex (vaginal, anus or mouth) until you and your partner(s) have finished treatment and tests have shown treatment has worked. BPG can prevent syphilis from being passed from a mother to baby. Babies born with syphilis (congenital syphilis), or babies whose mother had untreated syphilis, need to be treated right away to avoid serious health problems. Aqueous benzyl penicillin or procaine penicillin is recommended in infants with confirmed syphilis or infants who are clinically healthy but whose mothers had untreated syphilis, inadequately treated syphilis (including treatment within 30 days of giving birth), or syphilis treated with non-penicillin medicines. Unfortunately, while Syphilis can heal, there is no way to repair organs damaged by syphilis.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis develops in stages. The symptoms vary with each stage. But the stages may overlap. And the symptoms don't always happen in the same order. You may be infected with syphilis bacteria without noticing any symptoms for years. Primary syphilis: The first symptom of syphilis is a small sore called a chancre (SHANG-kur) that appears 2-12 weeks after exposure to someone with Syphilis. The sore is often painless. It appears at the spot where the bacteria entered your body. Most people with syphilis develop only one chancre. Some people get more than one. The chancre often forms about three weeks after you come in contact with syphilis bacteria. Many people who have syphilis don't notice the chancre. That's because it's usually painless. It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. It usually starts on the body's trunk, including chest, stomach, pelvis, back, and limbs. In time, it also could appear on the limbs, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Besides the rash, other symptoms may include wartlike sores, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Symptoms of secondary syphilis may go away on their own. But without treatment, they could come and go for months or years. Latent syphilis: If you aren't treated for syphilis, the disease moves from the secondary stage to the latent stage. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Tertiary syphilis: After the latent stage, up to 30% to 40% of people with syphilis who don't get treatment have complications known as tertiary syphilis. Here, they may develop permanently damaged heart, brain, muscles, bones, and eyes. Congenital syphilis: Pregnant people who have syphilis can pass the disease to their babies. Unborn babies can become infected through the organ that provides nutrients and oxygen in the womb, called the placenta. Infection also can happen during birth. Newborns with congenital syphilis might have no symptoms. But without fast treatment, some babies might get sores and rashes on the skin, fever, a type of discolored skin and eyes called jaundice, not enough red blood cells (anemia), swollen spleen and liver, sneezing or a stuffed, drippy nose called rhinitis, bone changes, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

It can infect the throat (from oral sex) or the rectum (from anal sex) or can manifest as an eye infection (gonoccocal conjuctivitis) in new born babies. Disseminated Gonococcal Infection is a more severe form where the infection spreads throughout the body. Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

When a person has active herpes lesions (a.k.a. blisters, sores, ulcers), your healthcare provider may diagnose genital herpes by simply looking at any sores that are present, or a swab can be taken and tests done that can detect the virus directly. Viral culture is even less accurate during recurrences (positive in only about 30% of recurrent outbreaks). NAAT methods are the preferred method, with PCR as the most-widely used NAAT method. These tests are fast, accurate, and can tell if a person has HSV-1 or HSV-2. There is also less chance of a false negative result with NAATs. Blood tests do not actually detect the virus but look for antibodies.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis develops in stages. The symptoms vary with each stage. But the stages may overlap. And the symptoms don't always happen in the same order. You may be infected with syphilis bacteria without noticing any symptoms for years. Primary syphilis: The first symptom of syphilis is a small sore called a chancre (SHANG-kur) that appears 2-12 weeks after exposure to someone with Syphilis. The sore is often painless. It appears at the spot where the bacteria entered your body. Most people with syphilis develop only one chancre. Some people get more than one. The chancre often forms about three weeks after you come in contact with syphilis bacteria. Many people who have syphilis don't notice the chancre. That's because it's usually painless. It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. It usually starts on the body's trunk, including chest, stomach, pelvis, back, and limbs. In time, it also could appear on the limbs, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Besides the rash, other symptoms may include wartlike sores, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Symptoms of secondary syphilis may go away on their own. But without treatment, they could come and go for months or years. Latent syphilis: If you aren't treated for syphilis, the disease moves from the secondary stage to the latent stage. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Tertiary syphilis: After the latent stage, up to 30% to 40% of people with syphilis who don't get treatment have complications known as tertiary syphilis. Here, they may develop permanently damaged heart, brain, muscles, bones, and eyes. Congenital syphilis: Pregnant people who have syphilis can pass the disease to their babies. Unborn babies can become infected through the organ that provides nutrients and oxygen in the womb, called the placenta. Infection also can happen during birth. Newborns with congenital syphilis might have no symptoms. But without fast treatment, some babies might get sores and rashes on the skin, fever, a type of discolored skin and eyes called jaundice, not enough red blood cells (anemia), swollen spleen and liver, sneezing or a stuffed, drippy nose called rhinitis, bone changes, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

TargetRLF1: Gonorrhea can be traced back to the earliest records of the human race. The Romans, Jews and Arabs all have documents referring to gonorrhea and each society had their own description of symptoms and treatment. The origins of Gonorrhea can be traced back to the Old Testament in the books of Leviticus and Genesis where it is described as a contagious, continuous passing out of semen and painful erection. The disease has been referred to by various names in different societies. The Roman physician Galen in 130 AD described the disease as an "involuntary escape of semen".   Hippocrates (460–375 BC) called it "Strangury." The disease was also referred to as “The Clap,” referring either to the “clapping” feeling experienced by the infected person during urination. In those days, men were considered victims and women as the source of the disease. The organism that causes the disease was first discovered in 1879 in Albert Neisser, hence the organisma being called Neisseria Gonorrhoea. The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis, or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing. Results are usually ready in a day. If bacteria are present, it indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of Chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for Chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely, the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear, and you may need to give another sample.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis develops in stages. The symptoms vary with each stage. But the stages may overlap. And the symptoms don't always happen in the same order. You may be infected with syphilis bacteria without noticing any symptoms for years. It appears at the spot where the bacteria entered your body. Most people with syphilis develop only one chancre. Some people get more than one. The chancre often forms about three weeks after you come in contact with syphilis bacteria. Many people who have syphilis don't notice the chancre. That's because it's usually painless. It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. It usually starts on the body's trunk, including chest, stomach, pelvis, back, and limbs. In time, it also could appear on the limbs, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Besides the rash, other symptoms may include wartlike sores, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Symptoms of secondary syphilis may go away on their own. But without treatment, they could come and go for months or years. Latent syphilis: If you aren't treated for syphilis, the disease moves from the secondary stage to the latent stage. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Tertiary syphilis: After the latent stage, up to 30% to 40% of people with syphilis who don't get treatment have complications known as tertiary syphilis. Here, they may develop permanently damaged heart, brain, muscles, bones, and eyes. Congenital syphilis: Pregnant people who have syphilis can pass the disease to their babies. Unborn babies can become infected through the organ that provides nutrients and oxygen in the womb, called the placenta. Infection also can happen during birth. Newborns with congenital syphilis might have no symptoms. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

TargetRLF1: Chlamydia infections also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary Infections spread through sexual contact, when vaginal fluid or semen containing the bacteria that causes chlamydia travels from one person to another. Sexual contact includes all kinds of sex, including sex that doesn’t involve penetration or ejaculation. There are lots of ways that the fluids from one person’s genitals can transmit the bacteria that causes chlamydia. Intercourse; bacteria pass from one person’s penis to their partner’s vagina or vice versa. Anal sex; bacteria pass from one person’s penis to their partner’s anus or vice versa. Sex involving toys; bacteria pass from a toy to a person’s mouth, penis, vagina or anus or through sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time they are used. Oral sex; bacteria pass from one person’s mouth to their partner’s penis, vagina or anus, or vice versa. Manual stimulation of the genitals or anus; less commonly, infected vaginal fluid or semen can come in contact with a person’s eye, causing an infection called conjunctivitis (pink eye). For example, this can happen if you touch the genitals of an infected person and then rub your eyes without washing your hands first. A pregnant person with chlamydia can give the infection to their baby during childbirth and that can cause a type of eye infection in the baby which can damage their sight.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.
